<meta>The text continues the dialogue between Confucius and the recluse Zi Sanghu from the previous section, focusing on the themes of detachment and the hardships of worldly life.</meta>

<margin>This describes the conduct of the Perfect Man <note>original: "zhiren"</note> who does not seek to be known or achieve worldly status. Why then, sir, do you take such joy in being heard of?</margin>
He rebuked him: "The Perfect Man remains unheard of; why do you rejoice in fame?" Confucius said: "How excellent!" He then declined 

<margin>He does not value superficial display.</margin>
social invitations, dismissed his disciples, and fled to the great marshes. He wore clothes made of coarse fur and hemp and ate acorns and chestnuts. 

<margin>He does not value rare delicacies.</margin>
<margin>He does not give rise to a mind of discrimination, and so he does not disturb the flocks of birds and beasts.</margin>
He entered among the beasts without disturbing the herd and among the birds without disturbing their flight. If even the birds and beasts did not dislike him, how much less would 

<margin>Even different species do not dislike him.</margin>
<margin>Surname and name of a recluse.</margin>
men? Confucius asked Zi Sanghu <note>a Daoist recluse known for his simple lifestyle</note>: "I was twice driven out of Lu, had a tree felled on me in Song, had my footprints wiped away in Wei, was reduced to poverty in Shang and Zhou, and was besieged between Chen and Cai. Having encountered these many calamities, my close friends have become increasingly distant and my followers have increasingly scattered. Why is this?" Zi Sanghu 

<note>A small printer's mark or seal is located in the top right corner of the page.</note>

<summary>Confucius adopts the lifestyle of a recluse after being rebuked for seeking fame, leading to a discussion with Zi Sanghu about his many political failures and social isolation.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Zi Sanghu, Perfect Man, recluses, Lu, Song, Wei, Chen, Cai, social isolation</keywords>
